title: TCP Extensions for High Performance
summary: Presents TCP extensions to improve performance over paths with large bandwidth-delay products and to give reliable operation over very high-speed paths. It defines new TCP options for this purpose. It was replaced by RFC 7323.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP was built for slow links, and by 1992 the new fiber connections had outgrown it. This RFC adds two options to TCP. One lets a receiver accept more than 64 KB of unacknowledged data at a time. The other adds a timestamp to each segment, so the sender can measure the delay of each round trip and the receiver can throw away very old duplicate data. Both options are agreed when the connection opens, so a computer that does not know them can still connect.

questions: what is the tcp timestamps option
subtitle: Two TCP options that let a fast link use a bigger window and time every round trip.

tldr.problem: TCP reports its receive window in a 16-bit field, so a connection can hold at most 65K bytes of unacknowledged data. On a fast link with a long delay that limit stalls the sender, and high speed also lets the 32-bit sequence numbers wrap around while old data is still in the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two TCP options. The window scale option carries a shift count agreed in the SYN segment that multiplies the window. The timestamps option carries a clock value in every segment, so the sender can measure the round-trip time and the receiver can reject old duplicate segments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1323 was a Proposed Standard from May 1992 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7323, which restates the same two options as its own document.

facts.label: Timestamps header overhead
facts.value: 12 bytes added to the 20-byte TCP header

today: RFC 1323 is a Proposed Standard from May 1992, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7323, which describes the same window scale and timestamps options as its own document. The RFC itself notes that it superseded RFC 1072 and RFC 1185, and its security considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Why TCP Needed Extending
sections.content:
TCP's performance depends on the product of the link rate and the round-trip delay, the bandwidth-delay product. That product is the amount of data that can be in flight at once, and TCP needs a receive window at least that large to keep a fast link busy. The 16-bit window field in the TCP header caps the window at 216 = 65K bytes, so on a long path with a fast link the sender repeatedly runs out of window and waits.

Two more problems follow from high speed. The 32-bit sequence number space can wrap around while a segment is still delayed in the network, and an old duplicate then lands inside the current window and looks like new data, corrupting the stream without any checksum error. And the round-trip time is sampled only about once per window, which on a long fat path gives a poor estimate and causes needless retransmissions.

The RFC also names selective acknowledgments, which would let a sender recover from several losses in one window, but leaves them out because their format and meaning were not yet settled. The extensions here are deliberately modest so that they can be added to a working protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP keeps a fixed amount of data in flight, set by a 16-bit number in the header, so at most 65K bytes. On a fast link with a long delay that is too little, and the sender waits. Higher speeds also make the 32-bit sequence numbers wrap around while old data is still crossing the network. The RFC adds two options to deal with both problems.

sections.title: The Window Scale Option
sections.content:
The window scale option is a three-byte TCP option with Kind 3, Length 3 and a single byte called shift.cnt. It has two purposes: it tells the peer that this TCP is prepared to scale windows in both directions, and it carries the scale factor to apply to the receiver's own window. The factor is a power of two, so it can be applied with a shift.

Both sides must send the option in their SYN segment for scaling to work in either direction, and the factor is then fixed for the life of the connection. A TCP that receives a SYN carrying the option replies with its own option in the SYN,ACK. A Window Scale option in a segment without the SYN bit must be ignored, and the window field inside a SYN segment is never scaled. Sending the option is an offer rather than a promise: a TCP that is ready to scale sends it even when its own shift count is zero.

The implementation rule is short. Keep the send window, receive window and congestion window as 32-bit numbers internally. Left-shift the incoming window field by the sender's scale before using it, and right-shift the outgoing window field by the receiver's scale before sending it. The shift count is limited to 14, which allows a window of 230 = 1 Gbyte; a peer that offers more than 14 should be treated as offering 14. The scale applies only to the transmitted window field, so it does not quantize the congestion window.
sections.plainLanguage: The window scale option is three bytes long and travels only in the opening segment of the connection. Each side states how far to shift the window number it reports, so a window can reach up to 1 Gbyte instead of stopping at 65K bytes. The shift is agreed once and cannot change later, and both sides must offer the option before either one uses it.

sections.title: The Timestamps Option
sections.content:
The timestamps option has Kind 8 and Length 10 bytes. It carries two four-byte fields: TSval, the current value of the sender's timestamp clock, and TSecr, a copy of a timestamp value the peer sent earlier. TSecr is only meaningful when the ACK bit is set in the TCP header; when it is not valid its value must be zero. The option is always sent and echoed in both directions, which keeps the mechanism simple and symmetric.

A TCP may send the option in the first SYN segment, and may then send it in other segments only if it received the option in the peer's first SYN. Because the option is 10 bytes long and TCP options are padded to a whole number of bytes, it adds 12 bytes to the 20-byte TCP header on every data or acknowledgment segment.

The clock itself is a 32-bit counter that must tick at least once for each 231 bytes sent. The RFC chooses a rate between 1 ms and 1 s per tick. A clock faster than one tick per second already rejects old duplicates on links of about 8 Gbps, and a 1 ms clock works up to 8 Tbps. The clock must also not wrap around faster than the maximum segment lifetime, which puts the fastest acceptable rate at one tick every 59 ns. The clock has to be monotonic: if the system clock jumps, an offset is added so the next value is never lower than the last.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamps option adds ten bytes to every segment that carries it. One field holds the sender's current clock reading, and the other carries back a reading the peer sent earlier. The counter must be steady and must not run through its full range too quickly, and the RFC settles on a tick every millisecond to every second.

sections.title: Measuring the Round-Trip Time
sections.content:
The sender puts its current clock value in TSval of each data segment, and the receiver copies that value into the TSecr field of the segment it sends back. When the sender receives an acknowledgment, it subtracts the echoed value from its own clock and gets the round-trip time for that segment. Because every segment carries a timestamp, the sender gets a fresh measurement for every acknowledgment instead of one per window, which is what makes accurate timing possible on a long path.

The receiver must pick which timestamp to echo, and the RFC gives three cases. When acknowledgments are delayed, the receiver should echo the timestamp of the earliest segment it has not yet acknowledged, so the measured delay includes the delay the receiver added. When a segment is missing, the receiver should echo the timestamp of the most recent segment that advanced the window, because a loss usually means the network is busy. When the hole is finally filled, it should echo the timestamp of the segment that filled it, because an older timestamp would include the sender's retransmission timeout and inflate the estimate.

The sender only uses an echoed timestamp to update its average round-trip time when the acknowledgment also advances the left edge of the send window. Without that rule, a pause in one direction would be counted as network delay and would push the sender into retransmitting too early.
sections.plainLanguage: Each data segment carries the sender's clock reading, and the receiver sends that reading back in its acknowledgment. The sender subtracts the returned value from its own clock and gets the delay of that round trip. The receiver follows three fixed rules about which reading to send back, so the number stays meaningful when segments are lost or acknowledgments are held back.

sections.title: Rejecting Old Duplicate Segments
sections.content:
PAWS, Protect Against Wrapped Sequence numbers, uses the same timestamps option to reject old duplicates. The receiver keeps the last timestamp it accepted. If an arriving segment carries a smaller timestamp than that, the segment is treated as an old duplicate: the receiver sends an acknowledgment and drops the segment. The timestamp is checked once, when the segment arrives, and a segment that is already queued is not checked again, so a full window of data in transit is not thrown away after a loss.

The timestamps are compared the same way sequence numbers are. Two values are ordered by their unsigned 32-bit difference, and one value counts as less than the other when that difference is above zero and below 231. The receiver does not need its clock synchronized with the sender's. It only treats the timestamp as a monotone serial number, effectively an extension of the high-order bits of the sequence number.

One edge case needs care. If a connection stays idle long enough for the peer's clock to pass the wrap point, the saved timestamp becomes meaningless and every later segment would be rejected, freezing the connection. The RFC therefore requires an implementation to invalidate the saved value after 24 days of idleness and to accept the next segment that arrives. It also recommends that reset segments carry no timestamps and be accepted whatever their timestamp, so that a reset can still clean up a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: PAWS is the rule that uses the timestamp to spot data that has been in the network too long. The receiver remembers the newest timestamp it accepted and drops any segment with an older one, after sending an acknowledgment. A connection that has been idle for more than 24 days clears that memory, so a stale clock reading cannot freeze the connection.

sections.title: Conclusions and Interoperability
sections.content:
All of the extensions travel in TCP options, and the RFC spends a section on staying compatible with hosts that do not implement them. Because a buggy implementation might crash the first time it met an option on a segment that was not a SYN, each extension is sent on non-SYN segments only after both sides have shown they understand it during the SYN exchange. A Window Scale or Timestamps option in a SYN,ACK is sent only if the matching option arrived in the first SYN.

The RFC says a vendor worried about overhead on slow links might turn the extensions off there. The timestamps option is the expensive one, because it rides on every data and acknowledgment segment; the window scale option costs nothing once the connection is open, because it appears only in the SYN.

The memo notes that it supersedes RFC 1072 and RFC 1185, and that the present form of the window scale option came from a later suggestion than the original one. Its security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Both extensions are negotiated in the opening segment of the connection and are only used afterwards if both ends asked for them. That way a computer that has never heard of them can still connect. The memo also notes that the window scale option came from an earlier suggestion and that it leaves security questions to other documents.

fields.name: Kind
fields.desc: Option kind. Set to 3 for the Window Scale option.

fields.name: shift.cnt
fields.desc: Shift count applied to the receive window. Limited to 14, which allows a window of 2^30 = 1 Gbyte.

fields.name: Kind
fields.desc: Option kind. Set to 8 for the Timestamps option.

fields.name: TSval
fields.desc: Current value of the sender's timestamp clock.

fields.name: TSecr
fields.desc: Copy of a timestamp value received from the peer. Valid only when the ACK bit is set.

messages.label: A: TSval=1, TSecr=120
messages.note: TCP A sends a data segment stamped with its current clock value.

messages.label: ACK(A): TSval=127, TSecr=1
messages.note: TCP B copies the received value into TSecr, so TCP A can measure the round trip.
